entries.1f8914ff0345afcffd841b1fd2ef9d8717fb365f: <div sID="gen24354" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Mark.2" sID="Mark.2"/> <div eID="gen24354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24355" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24356" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, we have, I. Christ's healing a man that was sick of a palsy, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.1-Mark.2.12">ver. 1-12</reference>. II. His calling of Matthew from the receipt of custom, and his eating, upon that occasion, with publicans and sinners, and justifying himself in so doing, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.13-Mark.2.17">ver. 13-17</reference>. III. His justifying his disciples in not fasting so much as those plucking the ears of corn on the sabbath day, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.23-Mark.2.28">ver. 23-28</reference>. All which passages we had before, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.1-Matt.9.38">Matt. ix.</reference> and <reference osisRef="Matt.12.1-Matt.12.50">xii.</reference>
entries.1cebd289c44695f73b962729c315c489ad085c83: <div eID="gen24356" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24355" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Healing of a Paralytic.</title> <div sID="gen24357" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And again he entered into Capernaum after <hi type="italic">some</hi> days; and it was noised that he was in the house. 2 And straightway many were gathered together, insomuch that there was no room to receive <hi type="italic">them,</hi> no, not so much as about the door: and he preached the word unto them. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they come unto him, bringing one sick of the palsy, which was borne of four. <hi type="super">4</hi> And when they could not come nigh unto him for the press, they uncovered the roof where he was: and when they had broken <hi type="italic">it</hi> up, they let down the bed wherein the sick of the palsy lay. <hi type="super">5</hi> When Jesus saw their faith, he said unto the sick of the palsy, Son, thy sins be forgiven thee. <hi type="super">6</hi> But there were certain of the scribes sitting there, and reasoning in their hearts, <hi type="super">7</hi> Why doth this <hi type="italic">man</hi> thus speak blasphemies? who can forgive sins but God only? <hi type="super">8</hi> And immediately when Jesus perceived in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, he said unto them, Why reason ye these things in your hearts? <hi type="super">9</hi> Whether is it easier to say to the sick of the palsy, <hi type="italic">Thy</hi> sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Arise, and take up thy bed, and walk? <hi type="super">10</hi> But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (he saith to the sick of the palsy,) <hi type="super">11</hi> I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy bed, and go thy way into thine house. <hi type="super">12</hi> And immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth before them all; insomuch that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, We never saw it on this fashion. <div eID="gen24357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24358" type="x-p"/> Christ, having been for some time preaching about in the country, here returns to Capernaum his head-quarters, and makes his appearance there, in hopes that by this time the talk and crowd would be somewhat abated. Now observe, <div eID="gen24358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24359" type="x-p"/> I. The great resort there was to him. Though he was <hi type="italic">in the house,</hi> wither Peter's house, or some lodgings of his own which he had taken, yet people came to him as soon as it was <hi type="italic">noised</hi> that he was in town; they did not stay till he appeared in the synagogue, which they might be sure he would do on the <hi type="italic">sabbath day,</hi> but <hi type="italic">straightway many were gathered together to him.</hi> Where the king is, there is the court; where Shiloh is, there <hi type="italic">shall the gathering of the people be.</hi> In improving opportunities for our souls, we must take care not to <hi type="italic">lose time.</hi> One invited another (Come, let us go see Jesus), so that his house could not contain his visitants. <hi type="italic">There was no room to receive them,</hi> they were so numerous, <hi type="italic">no not so much as about the door.</hi> A blessed sight, to see people thus flying like a cloud to Christ's house, though it was but a poor one, and <hi type="italic">as the doves to their windows!</hi> <div eID="gen24359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24360" type="x-p"/> II. The good entertainment Christ gave them, the best his house would afford, and better than any other could; he <hi type="italic">preached the word unto them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.2.2">v. 2</reference>. Many of them perhaps came only for cures, and many perhaps only for curiosity, to get a sight of him; but when he had them together he <hi type="italic">preached to them.</hi> Though the synagogue-door was open to him at proper times, he thought it not at all amiss to preach in a house, on a week day; though some might reckon it both an improper place and an improper time. <hi type="italic">Blessed are ye that sow beside all waters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.20">Isa. xxxii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen24360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24361" type="x-p"/> III. The presenting of a poor cripple to him, to be helped by him. The patient was one <hi type="italic">sick of the palsy,</hi> it should seem not as that, <reference osisRef="Matt.8.6">Matt. viii. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">grievously tormented,</hi> but perfectly disabled, so that he was <hi type="italic">borne of four,</hi> was carried upon <hi type="italic">a bed,</hi> as if he had been upon <hi type="italic">a bier,</hi> by four persons. It was his misery, that he needed to be so carried, and bespeaks the calamitous state of human life; it was their charity, who did so carry him, and bespeaks the compassion that it is justly expected should be in the children of men toward their fellow-creatures in distress, because we know not how soon the distress may be <hi type="italic">our own.</hi> These kind relations or neighbours thought, if they could but carry this poor man once to Christ, they should not need to carry him any more; and therefore made hard shift to get him to him; and when they could not otherwise get to him, they <hi type="italic">uncovered the roof where he was,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.2.4">v. 4</reference>. I see no necessity to conclude that Christ was preaching in an <hi type="italic">upper room,</hi> though in such the Jews that had stately houses, had their oratories; for then to what purpose should the crowd stand <hi type="italic">before the door,</hi> as wisdom's clients used to do? <reference osisRef="Prov.8.34">Prov. viii. 34</reference>. But I rather conjecture that the house he was in, was so little and mean (agreeable to his present state), that it had no <hi type="italic">upper room,</hi> but the <hi type="italic">ground-floor</hi> was open to the roof: and these petitioners for the poor paralytic, resolving not to be disappointed, when they could not get through the crowd at the door, got their friend by some means or other to the roof of the house, took off some of the tiles, and so let him down upon his bed with cords into the house where Christ was preaching. This bespoke both their <hi type="italic">faith</hi> and their <hi type="italic">fervency</hi> in this address to Christ. Hereby it appeared that they were in earnest, and would not go away, nor <hi type="italic">let Christ go without a blessing.</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.32.26">Gen. xxxii. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen24361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24362" type="x-p"/> IV. The kind word Christ said to this poor patient; <hi type="italic">He saw their faith;</hi> perhaps not so much his, for his distemper hindered him from the exercise of faith, but <hi type="italic">theirs</hi> that brought him. In curing the centurion's servant, Christ took notice of it as an instance of <hi type="italic">his faith,</hi> that he did not bring him to Christ, but believed he could cure him at a distance; here he commended <hi type="italic">their faith,</hi> because they did bring their friend through so much difficulty. Note, True faith and strong faith may work variously, conquering sometimes the objections of reason, sometimes those of sense; but, however manifested, it shall be accepted and approved by Jesus Christ. Christ said, <hi type="italic">Son, thy sins be forgiven thee.</hi> The <hi type="italic">compellation</hi> is very <hi type="italic">tender-Son;</hi> intimating a fatherly <hi type="italic">care</hi> of him and <hi type="italic">concern</hi> for him. Christ owns true believers as his sons: <hi type="italic">a son,</hi> and yet sick of the palsy. Herein God <hi type="italic">deals with you as with sons.</hi> The <hi type="italic">cordial</hi> is very rich; <hi type="italic">Thy sins are forgiven thee.</hi> Note, 1. Sin is the procuring cause of all our pains and sicknesses. The word of Christ was to take his thoughts off from the disease, which was the effect, and to lead them to the sin, the cause, that he might be more concerned about that, to get that pardoned. 2. God doth <hi type="italic">then</hi> graciously take away the sting and malignity of sickness, when he forgives sin; recovery from sickness is <hi type="italic">then</hi> a mercy indeed, when way is made for it by the pardon of sin. See <reference osisRef="Isa.38.17">Isa. xxxviii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Ps. ciii. 3</reference>. The way to remove the effect, is, to take away the cause. Pardon of sin strikes at the root of all diseases, and either cures them, or alters their property. <div eID="gen24362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24363" type="x-p"/> V. The cavil of the scribes at that which Christ said, and a demonstration of the unreasonableness of their cavil. They were expositors of the law, and their doctrine was <hi type="italic">true</hi>—that it is blasphemy for any creature to undertake the pardon of sin, and that it is God's prerogative, <reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Isa. xliii. 25</reference>. But, as is usual with such teachers, their application was <hi type="italic">false,</hi> and was the effect of their ignorance and enmity to Christ. It is <hi type="italic">true, None can forgive sins but God only;</hi> but it is false that therefore Christ cannot, who had abundantly proved himself to have a divine power. But Christ <hi type="italic">perceived in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves;</hi> this proves him to be God, and therefore confirmed what was to be proved, that he had authority to <hi type="italic">forgive sins;</hi> for he <hi type="italic">searched</hi> the heart, and knew <hi type="italic">what was in man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.23">Rev. ii. 23</reference>. God's royalties are inseparable, and he that could <hi type="italic">know thoughts,</hi> could <hi type="italic">forgive sins.</hi> This magnifies the grace of Christ, in <hi type="italic">pardoning sin,</hi> that he knew men's thoughts, and therefore knows more than any other can know, both of the sinfulness of their sins and the particulars of them, and yet is ready to pardon. Now he proves his power to <hi type="italic">forgive sin,</hi> by demonstrating his power to cure the <hi type="italic">man sick of the palsy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.2.9-Mark.2.11">v. 9-11</reference>. He would not have pretended to do <hi type="italic">the one,</hi> if he could not have done <hi type="italic">the other; that ye may know that the Son of man,</hi> the Messiah, <hi type="italic">has power on earth to forgive sin,</hi> that I have that power, <hi type="italic">Thou that art</hi> sick of the palsy, <hi type="italic">arise, take up thy bed.</hi> Now, 1. This was a <hi type="italic">suitable</hi> argument in itself. He could not have cured the disease, which was the effect, if he could not have taken away the sin, which was the cause. And besides, his curing diseases was a figure of his pardoning sin, for sin is the disease of the soul; when it is pardoned, it is healed. He that could by a word accomplish the sign, could doubtless perform the thing signified, 2. It was suited to them. These carnal scribes would be more affected with such a suitable effect of a pardon as the cure of the disease, and be sooner convinced by it, than by any other more spiritual consequences; therefore it was proper enough to appeal, whether it is easier to say, <hi type="italic">Thy sins are forgiven thee,</hi> or to say, <hi type="italic">Arise, and walk?</hi> The removing of the punishment as such, was the remitting of the sin; he that could go so far in the cure, no doubt could perfect it. See <reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Isa. xxxiii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen24363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24364" type="x-p"/> VI. The cure of the sick man, and the impression it made upon the people, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.12">v. 12</reference>. He not only <hi type="italic">arise</hi> out of his bed, perfectly well, but, to show that he had perfect strength restored to him, <hi type="italic">he took up his bed,</hi> because it lay in the way, <hi type="italic">and went forth before them all;</hi> and <hi type="italic">they were all amazed,</hi> as well they might, and <hi type="italic">glorified God,</hi> as indeed they ought; saying, "<hi type="italic">We never saw it on this fashion;</hi> never were such wonders as these done before in our time." Note, Christ's works were without precedent. When we see what he does in healing souls, we must own that we <hi type="italic">never saw the like.</hi>
entries.44e1964b652e1da1f5158787537845e70ba7bce5: <div eID="gen24364" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ among Publicans and Sinners.</title> <div sID="gen24365" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And he went forth again by the sea side; and all the multitude resorted unto him, and he taught them. <hi type="super">14</hi> And as he passed by, he saw Levi the <hi type="italic">son</hi> of Alphæus sitting at the receipt of custom, and said unto him, Follow me. And he arose and followed him. <hi type="super">15</hi> And it came to pass, that, as Jesus sat at meat in his house, many publicans and sinners sat also together with Jesus and his disciples: for there were many, and they followed him. <hi type="super">16</hi> And when the scribes and Pharisees saw him eat with publicans and sinners, they said unto his disciples, How is it that he eateth and drinketh with publicans and sinners? 17 When Jesus heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> he saith unto them, They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. <div eID="gen24365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24366" type="x-p"/> Here is, <div eID="gen24366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24367" type="x-p"/> I. Christ preaching by the <hi type="italic">sea-side</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.13">v. 13</reference>), whither he went <hi type="italic">for room,</hi> because he found, upon second trial, no house or street large enough to contain his auditory; but upon the strand there might come as many as would. It should seem by this, that our Lord Jesus had a strong voice, and could and did speak loud; for <hi type="italic">wisdom crieth without</hi> in the <hi type="italic">places of concourse.</hi> Wherever he goes, though it be to the sea-side, <hi type="italic">multitudes resort to him.</hi> Wherever the doctrine of Christ is faithfully preached, though it be driven into corners or into deserts, we must follow it. <div eID="gen24367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24368" type="x-p"/> II. His calling Levi; the same with Matthew, who had a place in the custom-house at Capernaum, from which he was denominated a <hi type="italic">publican;</hi> his place fixed him by the water-side, and thither Christ went to meet with him, and to give him an effectual call. This Levi is here said to be <hi type="italic">the son of Alpheus</hi> or <hi type="italic">Cleophas,</hi> husband to that Mary who was sister or near kinswoman to the virgin Mary and if so, he was own brother to James the less, and Jude, and Simon the Canaanite, so that there were four brothers of them apostles, It is probable that Matthew was but a loose extravagant young man, or else, being a Jew, he would never have been a publican. However, Christ called him to <hi type="italic">follow him.</hi> Paul, though a Pharisee, had been one of the chief of sinners, and yet was called to be an apostle. With God, through Christ, there is mercy to pardon the greatest sins, and grace to sanctify the greatest sinners. Matthew, that had been a publican, became an evangelist, the <hi type="italic">first</hi> that put pen to paper, and the <hi type="italic">fullest</hi> in writing the life of Christ. Great sin and scandal before conversion, are no bar to great gifts, graces, and advancements, after; nay, God may be the more glorified. Christ prevented him with this call; in bodily cures, ordinarily, he was <hi type="italic">sought unto,</hi> but in these spiritual cures, he was <hi type="italic">found of them that sought him not.</hi> For this is the great evil and peril of the disease of sin, that those who are under it, desire not to be <hi type="italic">made whole.</hi> <div eID="gen24368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24369" type="x-p"/> III. His familiar converse with <hi type="italic">publicans and sinners,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.2.15">v. 15</reference>. We are here told, 1. That Christ <hi type="italic">sat at meat in Levi's house,</hi> who invited <hi type="italic">him and his disciples</hi> to the farewell-feast he made to his friends, when he left all to attend on Christ: such a feast he made, as Elisha did (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.21">1 Kings xix. 21</reference>), to show, not only with what cheerfulness in himself, but with what thankfulness to God, he quitted all, in compliance with Christ's call. Fitly did he make the <hi type="italic">day of his espousals</hi> to Christ a festival day. This was also to testify his respect to Christ, and the grateful sense he had of his kindness, in snatching him from the receipt of custom as a brand out of the burning. 2. That <hi type="italic">many publicans and sinners</hi> sat with Christ in Levi's house (for <hi type="italic">there were many</hi> belonging to that custom-house); and <hi type="italic">they followed him.</hi> They followed Levi; so some understand it, supposing that, like Zaccheus, he was <hi type="italic">chief among the publicans,</hi> and was <hi type="italic">rich;</hi> and for that reason, the inferior sort of them attended him for what they could get. I rather take it, that they <hi type="italic">followed Jesus</hi> because of the report they had heard of him. They did not <hi type="italic">for conscience-sake</hi> leave all to follow him, but <hi type="italic">for curiosity-sake</hi> they came to Levi's feast, to see him; whatever brought them thither, they were sitting with <hi type="italic">Jesus and his disciples.</hi> The publicans are here and elsewhere ranked with <hi type="italic">sinners,</hi> the worst of <hi type="italic">sinners.</hi> (1.) Because commonly they <hi type="italic">were such;</hi> so general were the corruptions in the execution of that office, oppressing, exacting, and taking bribes or fees to extortion, and <hi type="italic">accusing falsely,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.13-Luke.3.14">Luke iii. 13, 14</reference>. A faithful fair-dealing publican was so rare, even at Rome, that one Sabinus, who kept a clean reputation in that office, was, after his death, honoured with this inscription, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Kalos telonesanti</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Here lies an honest publican.</hi> (2.) Because the Jews had a particular antipathy to them and their office, as an affront to the liberty of their nation and a badge of their slavery, and therefore put them into an ill name, and thought it scandalous to be seen in their company. Such as these our blessed Lord was pleased to converse with, when he appeared <hi type="italic">in the likeness of sinful flesh.</hi> <div eID="gen24369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24370" type="x-p"/> IV. The <hi type="italic">offence</hi> which the scribes and Pharisees took at this, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.16">v. 16</reference>. They would not come to hear him preach, which they might have been convinced the edified by; but they would come themselves to <hi type="italic">see him</hi> sit with publicans and sinners, which they would be provoked by. They endeavoured to put the disciples out of conceit with their Master, as a man not of such sanctity and severe morals as became his character; and therefore put the question to them. <hi type="italic">How is it, that he eateth and drinketh with publicans and sinners?</hi> Note, It is no new thing for that which is both well-<hi type="italic">done,</hi> and well-<hi type="italic">designed,</hi> to be misrepresented, and turned to the reproach of the wisest and best of men. <div eID="gen24370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24371" type="x-p"/> V. Christ's justification of himself in it, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.17">v. 17</reference>. He stood to what he did, and would not withdraw, though the Pharisees were offended, as Peter afterwards did, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.12">Gal. ii. 12</reference>. Note, Those are too tender of their own <hi type="italic">good name,</hi> who, to preserve it with some nice people, will decline a <hi type="italic">good work.</hi> Christ would not do so. They thought the publicans were to be <hi type="italic">hated.</hi> "No," saith Christ, "they are to be <hi type="italic">pitied,</hi> they are <hi type="italic">sick</hi> and <hi type="italic">need a physician;</hi> they are sinners, and need a Saviour." They thought Christ's character should separate him from them; "No," saith Christ, "my commission directs me to them; <hi type="italic">I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.</hi> If the world had been <hi type="italic">righteous,</hi> there had been no occasion for my coming, either to <hi type="italic">preach</hi> repentance, or to <hi type="italic">purchase</hi> remission. It is to a <hi type="italic">sinful world</hi> that I am sent, and therefore my business lies most with those that are the greatest sinners in it." Or thus; "<hi type="italic">I am not come to call the righteous,</hi> the proud Pharisees that think themselves righteous, that ask, <hi type="italic">Wherein shall we return?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.7">Mal. iii. 7</reference>), Of what shall we repent? But poor publicans, that own themselves to be sinners, and are glad to be invited and encouraged to repent." It is good dealing with those that there is hope of; now there is <hi type="italic">more hope of a fool</hi> than of one that is <hi type="italic">wise in his own conceit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.12">Prov. xxvi. 12</reference>.
entries.21885b721bbee9b56b7dc5485906d08a4e84ba2e: <div eID="gen24371" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Hypocritical Rigour of the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen24372" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> And the disciples of John and of the Pharisees used to fast: and they come and say unto him, Why do the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, but thy disciples fast not? <hi type="super">19</hi> And Jesus said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them? as long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. <hi type="super">20</hi> But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast in those days. <hi type="super">21</hi> No man also seweth a piece of new cloth on an old garment: else the new piece that filled it up taketh away from the old, and the rent is made worse. <hi type="super">22</hi> And no man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles, and the wine is spilled, and the bottles will be marred: but new wine must be put into new bottles. <hi type="super">23</hi> And it came to pass, that he went through the corn fields on the sabbath day; and his disciples began, as they went, to pluck the ears of corn. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the Pharisees said unto him, Behold, why do they on the sabbath day that which is not lawful? <hi type="super">25</hi> And he said unto them, Have ye never read what David did, when he had need, and was an hungred, he, and they that were with him? <hi type="super">26</hi> How he went into the house of God in the days of Abiathar the high priest, and did eat the showbread, which is not lawful to eat but for the priests, and gave also to them which were with him? <hi type="super">27</hi> And he said unto them, The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath: <hi type="super">28</hi> Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath. <div eID="gen24372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24373" type="x-p"/> Christ had been put to <hi type="italic">justify</hi> himself in conversing with <hi type="italic">publicans and sinners:</hi> here he is put to justify his disciples; and in what they do according to his will he will justify them, and bear them out. <div eID="gen24373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24374" type="x-p"/> I. He justifies them in their <hi type="italic">not fasting,</hi> which was turned to their reproach by the Pharisees. Why do the Pharisees and the disciples of John fast? They <hi type="italic">used to fast,</hi> the Pharisees fasted <hi type="italic">twice in the week</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.12">Luke xviii. 12</reference>), and probably the disciples of John did so too; and, it should seem, this very day, when Christ and his disciples were feasting in Levi's house, was their <hi type="italic">fast-day,</hi> for the word is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">nesteuousi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">they do fast,</hi> or <hi type="italic">are fasting,</hi> which aggravated the offence. Thus apt are strict professors to make their own practice a standard, and to censure and condemn all that do not fully come up to it. They invidiously suggest that if Christ went among sinners to do them <hi type="italic">good,</hi> as he had pleaded, yet the disciples went to indulge their appetites, for they never knew what it was to fast, or to deny themselves. Note, Ill-will always suspects the worst. <div eID="gen24374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24375" type="x-p"/> Two things Christ pleads in excuse of his disciples <hi type="italic">not fasting.</hi> <div eID="gen24375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24376" type="x-p"/> 1. That these were <hi type="italic">easy days</hi> with them, and fasting was not so <hi type="italic">seasonable</hi> now as it would be hereafter, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.19-Mark.2.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. There is a time for all things. Those that enter into the married state, must expect care and <hi type="italic">trouble in the flesh,</hi> and yet, during the nuptial solemnity, they are merry, and think it becomes them to be so; it was very absurd for Samson's bride to <hi type="italic">weep before</hi> him, <hi type="italic">during the days that the feast lasted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.14.17">Judg. xiv. 17</reference>. Christ and his disciples were but newly married, the bridegroom was <hi type="italic">yet with them,</hi> the nuptials were yet in the celebrating (Matthew's particularly); when the bridegroom should be removed from them to the far country, about his business, then would be a proper time to sit as a widow, in solitude and fasting. <div eID="gen24376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24377" type="x-p"/> 2. That these were <hi type="italic">early days</hi> with them, and they were not so able for the severe exercises of religion as hereafter they would be. The Pharisees had long accustomed themselves to such austerities; and John Baptist himself came neither eating nor drinking. His disciples from the first inured themselves to hardships, and thus found it easier to bear strict and frequent fasting, but it was not so with Christ's disciples; their Master came <hi type="italic">eating and drinking,</hi> and had not bred them up to the difficult services of religion as yet, for it was all in good time. To put them upon such frequent fasting at first, would be a discouragement to them, and perhaps drive them off from following Christ; it would be of as ill consequence as <hi type="italic">putting new wine into old casks,</hi> or sewing <hi type="italic">new cloth</hi> to that which is worn thin and threadbare, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.21-Mark.2.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. Note, God graciously <hi type="italic">considers the frame</hi> of young Christians, that are <hi type="italic">weak</hi> and <hi type="italic">tender,</hi> and so must we; nor must we expect more than the <hi type="italic">work of the day in its day,</hi> and that day according to the strength, because it is not in our hands to give strength according to the day. Many contract an antipathy to some kind of food, otherwise good, by being surfeited with it when they are young; so, many entertain prejudices against the exercises of devotion by being burthened with them, and <hi type="italic">made to serve with an offering,</hi> at their setting out. Weak Christians must take heed of <hi type="italic">over-tasking</hi> themselves, and of making the yoke of Christ otherwise than as it is, easy, and sweet, and pleasant. <div eID="gen24377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24378" type="x-p"/> II. He justifies them in <hi type="italic">plucking the ears of corn on the sabbath day,</hi> which, I will warrant you, a disciples of the Pharisees would not dare to have done; for it was contrary to an express tradition of their elders. In this instance, as in that before, they reflect upon the discipline of Christ's school, as if it were not so strict as that of theirs: so common it is for those who deny the <hi type="italic">power of godliness,</hi> to be jealous for the <hi type="italic">form,</hi> and censorious of those who affect not <hi type="italic">their</hi> form. <div eID="gen24378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24379" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. What a poor breakfast Christ's disciples had on a sabbath-day morning, when they were going to church (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.23">v. 23</reference>); they <hi type="italic">plucked the ears of corn,</hi> and that was the best they had. They were so intent upon spiritual dainties, that they forgot even their <hi type="italic">necessary food;</hi> and the word of Christ was to them instead of that; and their zeal for it even <hi type="italic">ate them up.</hi> The Jews made it a piece of religion, to eat dainty food on sabbath days, but the disciples were content with any thing. <div eID="gen24379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24380" type="x-p"/> 2. How even this was <hi type="italic">grudged them</hi> by the Pharisees, upon supposition that it was not lawful to <hi type="italic">pluck the ears of corn</hi> on the sabbath day, that that was as much a servile work as <hi type="italic">reaping</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.24">v. 24</reference>); <hi type="italic">Why do they on the sabbath day that which is not lawful?</hi> Note, If Christ's disciples do that which is unlawful, Christ will be reflected upon, and upbraided with it, as he was here, and dishonour will redound to his name. It is observable, that when the Pharisees thought Christ did amiss, they told the disciples (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.16">v. 16</reference>); and now when they thought the disciples did amiss, they spoke to Christ, as make-bates, that did what they could to sow discord between Christ and his disciples, and make a breach in the family. <div eID="gen24380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24381" type="x-p"/> 3. How Christ defended them in what they did. <div eID="gen24381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24382" type="x-p"/> (1.) By example. They had a good precedent for it in David's eating the <hi type="italic">show-bread,</hi> when he was hungry, and there was no other bread to be had (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.25-Mark.2.26">v. 25, 26</reference>); <hi type="italic">Have ye never read?</hi> Note, Many of our mistakes would be rectified, and our unjust censures of others corrected, if we would but recollect what <hi type="italic">we have read</hi> in the scripture; appeals to that are most convincing. "You have read that David, the man after God's own heart, <hi type="italic">when he was hungry,</hi> made no difficulty of eating <hi type="italic">the show-bread,</hi> which by the law none might eat of but the priests and their families." Note, Ritual observances must give way to moral obligations; and that may be done in a case of necessity, which otherwise may not be done. This, it is said, David did in the days of <hi type="italic">Abiathar the High-Priest;</hi> or <hi type="italic">just before</hi> the days of Abiathar, who immediately succeeded Abimelech his father in the pontificate, and, it is probable, was at that time his father's deputy, or assistant, in the office; and he it was that escaped the massacre, and brought the ephod to David. <div eID="gen24382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24383" type="x-p"/> (2.) By argument. To reconcile them to the disciples' <hi type="italic">plucking the ears of corn,</hi> let them consider, <div eID="gen24383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24384" type="x-p"/> [1.] Whom the sabbath was <hi type="italic">made for</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.27">v. 27</reference>); <hi type="italic">it was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.</hi> This we had not in Matthew. The sabbath is a sacred and divine institution; but we must receive and embrace it as a privilege and a benefit, not as a task and a drudgery. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> God never designed it to be an <hi type="italic">imposition</hi> upon us, and therefore we must not make it so to ourselves. <hi type="italic">Man was not made for the sabbath,</hi> for he was made a day before the sabbath was instituted. Man was made <hi type="italic">for God,</hi> and for his honour and service, and he just rather die than deny him; but he was not <hi type="italic">made for the sabbath,</hi> so as to be tied up by the law of it, from that which is necessary to the support of his life. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> God did design it to be an <hi type="italic">advantage</hi> to us, and so we must make it, and improve it. He made if <hi type="italic">for man.</hi> 1. He had <hi type="italic">some</hi> regard to our <hi type="italic">bodies</hi> in the institution, that they might rest, and not be tired out with the constant business of this world (<reference osisRef="Deut.5.14">Deut. v. 14</reference>); <hi type="italic">that thy man-servant and thy maid-servant may rest.</hi> Now he that intended the <hi type="italic">sabbath-rest</hi> for the <hi type="italic">repose</hi> of our bodies, certainly never intended it should restrain us, in a case of necessity, from fetching in the necessary <hi type="italic">supports</hi> of the body; it must be construed so as not to contradict itself—for <hi type="italic">edification,</hi> and not for <hi type="italic">destruction.</hi> 2. He had <hi type="italic">much more</hi> regard to our <hi type="italic">souls.</hi> The <hi type="italic">sabbath</hi> was made a day of rest, only in order to its being a day of holy work, a day of communion with God, a day of praise and thanksgiving; and the rest from worldly business is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> necessary, that we may closely apply ourselves to this work, and spend the whole time in it, in public and in private; but then time is allowed us for that which is necessary to the fitting of our bodies for the service of our souls in God's service, and the enabling of them to <hi type="italic">keep pace</hi> with them in that work. See here, (1.) What a <hi type="italic">good Master</hi> we serve, all whose institutions are for our own benefit, and if we be so wise as to observe them, we are <hi type="italic">wise for ourselves;</hi> it is not he, but we, that are gainers by our service. (2.) What we should aim at in our <hi type="italic">sabbath work,</hi> even the good of our own souls. If the sabbath was made for man, we should then ask ourselves at night, "What am I the better for this sabbath day?" (3.) What care we ought to take not to make those exercises of religion burthens to ourselves or others, which God ordained to be blessings; neither adding to the command by unreasonable strictness, nor indulging those corruptions which are adverse to the command, for thereby we make those devout exercises a penance to ourselves, which otherwise would be a pleasure. <div eID="gen24384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24385" type="x-p"/> [2.] Whom the sabbath was <hi type="italic">made by</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.28">v. 28</reference>); "<hi type="italic">The Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath;</hi> and therefore he will not see the kind intentions of the institution of it frustrated by your impositions." Note, The sabbath days are <hi type="italic">days of the Son of man;</hi> he is the Lord of the day, and to his honour it must be observed; by him God made the worlds, and so it was by him that the sabbath was first instituted; by him God gave the law at mount Sinai, and so the <hi type="italic">fourth</hi> commandment was <hi type="italic">his law;</hi> and that little alteration that was shortly to be made, by the shifting of it one day forward to the first day of the week, was to be in remembrance of <hi type="italic">his</hi> resurrection, and therefore the Christian sabbath was to be called <hi type="italic">the Lord's day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Rev. i. 10</reference>), the Lord Christ's day; and the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> Christ, as Mediator, is always to be looked upon as Lord of the sabbath. This argument he largely insists upon in his own justification, when he was charged with having broken the sabbath, <reference osisRef="John.5.16">John v. 16</reference>.  <chapter eID="Mark.2"/> <div eID="gen24385" type="x-p"/>

entries.e6cab7259ee650948f5cebd1f51c3b87cdca531e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13876"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.2.1-Mark.2.12">Mr 2:1-12</reference>. Healing of a Paralytic. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.9.1-Matt.9.8">Mt 9:1-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.5.17-Luke.5.26">Lu 5:17-26</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26692" type="x-p"/> This incident, as remarked on <reference osisRef="Matt.9.1">Mt 9:1</reference>, appears to follow next in order of time after the cure of the leper (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.40-Mark.1.45">Mr 1:40-45</reference>).<div eID="gen26692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13876"/><hi type="bold">1. And again he entered into Capernaum--</hi>"His own city" (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.1">Mt 9:1</reference>).<div eID="gen26693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and it was noised that he was in the house--</hi>no doubt of Simon Peter (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.29">Mr 1:29</reference>). <div eID="gen26694" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd21571ae760dd655ee78b096ce7857c178d8a8f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13877"/><div sID="gen26695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13877"/><hi type="bold">2. And straightway many were gathered together, insomuch that there was no room to receive them, no, not so much as about the door--</hi>This is one of Mark's graphic touches. No doubt in this case, as the scene occurred at his informant's own door, these details are the vivid recollections of that honored disciple.<div eID="gen26695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he preached the word unto them--</hi>that is, indoors; but in the hearing, doubtless, of the multitude that pressed around. Had He gone forth, as He naturally would, the paralytic's faith would have had no such opportunity to display itself. Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.17">Lu 5:17</reference>) furnishes an additional and very important incident in the scene--as follows: "And it came to pass on a certain day, as He was teaching, that there were Pharisees and doctors of the law sitting by, which were come out of every town," or village, "of Galilee, and Judea, and Jerusalem." This was the highest testimony yet borne to our Lord's growing influence, and the necessity increasingly felt by the ecclesiastics throughout the country of coming to some definite judgment regarding Him. "And the power of the Lord was [present] to heal them"--or, "was [efficacious] to heal them," that is, the sick that were brought before Him. So that the miracle that is now to be described was among the most glorious and worthy to be recorded of many then performed; and what made it so was doubtless the faith which was manifested in connection with it, and the proclamation of the forgiveness of the patient's sins that immediately preceded it. <div eID="gen26696" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bdc1791108fe4a7893a1e1a8c4cf1cc28fc597b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13878"/><div sID="gen26697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13878"/><hi type="bold">3. And they come unto him--</hi>that is, towards the house where He was.<div eID="gen26697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bringing one sick of the palsy--</hi>"lying on a bed" (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.2">Mt 9:2</reference>).<div eID="gen26698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which was borne of four--</hi>a graphic particular of Mark only. <div eID="gen26699" type="x-p"/>
entries.3311ab9858b212419959bfe9ac9fd0339e8f2ec2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13879"/><div sID="gen26700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13879"/><hi type="bold">4. And when they could not come nigh unto him for the press--</hi>or, as in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.19">Lu 5:19</reference>), "when they could not find by what way they might bring him in because of the multitude," they "went upon the housetop"--the flat or terrace-roof, universal in Eastern houses.<div eID="gen26700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they uncovered the roof where he was: and when they had broken it up, they let down the bed--</hi>or portable couch<div eID="gen26701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherein the sick of the palsy lay--</hi>Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.19">Lu 5:19</reference>) says, they "let him down through the tilling with his couch into the midst before Jesus." Their whole object was to bring the patient into the presence of Jesus; and this not being possible in the ordinary way, because of the multitude that surrounded Him, they took the very unusual method here described of accomplishing their object, and succeeded. Several explanations have been given of the way in which this was done; but unless we knew the precise plan of the house, and the part of it from which Jesus taught--which may have been a quadrangle or open court, within the buildings of which Peter's house was one, or a gallery covered by a veranda--it is impossible to determine precisely how the thing was done. One thing, however, is clear, that we have both the accounts from an eye-witness. <div eID="gen26702" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6ff66c1d6a43f34cbd719b0ea952bc49b73349e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13880"/><div sID="gen26703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13880"/><hi type="bold">5. When Jesus saw their faith--</hi>It is remarkable that all the three narratives call it "their faith" which Jesus saw. That the patient himself had faith, we know from the proclamation of his forgiveness, which Jesus made before all; and we should have been apt to conclude that his four friends bore him to Jesus merely out of benevolent compliance with the urgent entreaties of the poor sufferer. But here we learn, not only that his bearers had the same faith with himself, but that Jesus marked it as a faith which was not to be defeated--a faith victorious over all difficulties. This was the faith for which He was ever on the watch, and which He never saw without marking, and, in those who needed anything from Him, richly rewarding.<div eID="gen26703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he said unto the sick of the palsy, Son--</hi>"be of good cheer" (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.2">Mt 9:2</reference>).<div eID="gen26704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy sins be forgiven thee--</hi>By the word "be," our translators perhaps meant "are," as in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.20">Lu 5:20</reference>). For it is not a command to his sins to depart, but an authoritative proclamation of the man's pardoned state as a believer. And yet, as the Pharisees understood our Lord to be dispensing pardon by this saying, and Jesus not only acknowledges that they were right, but founds His whole argument upon the correctness of it, we must regard the saying as a royal proclamation of the man's forgiveness by Him to whom it belonged to dispense it; nor could such a style of address be justified on any lower supposition. (See on <reference osisRef="Luke.7.41">Lu 7:41</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen26705" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a5c14c8677d6dc45a2db16928db621dac1d4257: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13881"/><div sID="gen26706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13881"/><hi type="bold">6. But there were certain of the scribes--</hi>"and the Pharisees" (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.21">Lu 5:21</reference>)<div eID="gen26706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sitting there--</hi>those Jewish ecclesiastics who, as Luke told us (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.17">Lu 5:17</reference>), "were come out of every village of Galilee, and Judea, and Jerusalem," to make their observations upon this wonderful Person, in anything but a teachable spirit, though as yet their venomous and murderous feeling had not showed itself.<div eID="gen26707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26708" type="x-p"/> and reasoning in their hearts. <div eID="gen26708" type="x-p"/>
entries.706b8e903489ec3cfd2a3feaa23f5846515a7275: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13882"/><div sID="gen26709" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13882"/><hi type="bold">7. Why doth this man thus speak blasphemies? who can forgive sins but God only?--</hi>In this second question they expressed a great truth. (See <reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Is 43:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Ex 34:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.7">7</reference>, &c.). Nor was their first question altogether unnatural, though in our Lord's sole case it was unfounded. That a man, to all appearances like one of themselves, should claim authority and power to forgive sins, they could not, on the first blush of it, but regard as in the last degree startling; nor were they entitled even to weigh such a claim, as worthy of a hearing, save on supposition of resistless evidence afforded by Him in support of the claim. Accordingly, our Lord deals with them as men entitled to such evidence, and supplies it; at the same time chiding them for rashness, in drawing harsh conclusions regarding Himself. <div eID="gen26709" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d55e3ac530a91cee0fafea2c57d3e174be762f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13883"/><div sID="gen26710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13883"/><hi type="bold">8. Why reason ye these things in your hearts--</hi>or, as in Matthew, (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.4">Mt 9:4</reference>) "Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?" <div eID="gen26710" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5455d01bcc2e949fcabc63a841c23e515bf51f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13884"/><div sID="gen26711" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13884"/><hi type="bold">9. Whether is it easier to say to the sick of the palsy, Thy sins be forgiven thee--</hi>or "are forgiven thee";<div eID="gen26711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or to say, Arise, and take up thy bed and walk?--</hi>"Is it easier to command away disease than to bid away sin? If, then, I do the one which you can see, know thus that I have done the other, which you cannot see." <div eID="gen26712" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1b4e77be00c43c9aa5446cebfade160281903bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13885"/><div sID="gen26713" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13885"/><hi type="bold">10. But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins--</hi>that forgiving power dwells in the Person of this Man, and is exercised by Him while on this earth and going out and in with you.<div eID="gen26713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26714" type="x-p"/> (he saith to the sick of the palsy), <div eID="gen26714" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2867e8aea8b9a5d2f47dfbb24deaa5b3581e0fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13886"/><div sID="gen26715" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13886"/><hi type="bold">11. I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy bed, and go thy way into thine house--</hi>This taking up the portable couch, and walking home with it, was designed to prove the completeness of the cure. <div eID="gen26715" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee899a1702e85623def09f1357ceb129b8f08fbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13887"/><div sID="gen26716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13887"/><hi type="bold">12. And immediately he arose, took up the bed--</hi>"Sweet saying!" says Bengel: "The bed had borne the man: now the man bore the bed."<div eID="gen26716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and went forth before them all--</hi>proclaiming by that act to the multitude, whose wondering eyes would follow him as he pressed through them, that He who could work such a glorious miracle of healing, must indeed "have power on earth to forgive sins."<div eID="gen26717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We never saw it on this fashion--</hi>"never saw it thus," or, as we say, "never saw the like." In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.26">Lu 5:26</reference>) it is, "We have seen strange [unexpected] things to-day"--referring both to the miracles wrought and the forgiveness of sins pronounced by Human Lips. In Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.8">Mt 9:8</reference>) it is, "They marvelled, and glorified God, which had given such power unto men." At forgiving power they wondered not, but that a man, to all appearance like one of themselves, should possess it!<div eID="gen26718" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.2.13-Mark.2.17">Mr 2:13-17</reference>. entries.c8da568bec8d96e4ee4b398d4da7919d30da99b4: <div eID="gen39139" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39140" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39141" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39141" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39140" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39142" type="x-p"/> Christ preaches in Capernaum, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.1">Mar 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.2">Mar 2:2</reference>. A paralytic person is brought to him, whose sins are pronounced forgiven, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.3-Mar.2.5">Mar 2:3-5</reference>. The scribes accuse him of blasphemy, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.6">Mar 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.7">Mar 2:7</reference>. He vindicates himself, and proves his power to forgive sins, by healing the man's disease, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.8-Mar.2.11">Mar 2:8-11</reference>. The people are astonished and edified, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.12">Mar 2:12</reference>. He calls Levi from the receipt of custom, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.13">Mar 2:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.14">Mar 2:14</reference>. Eats in his house with publicans and sinners, at which the Pharisees murmur, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.15">Mar 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.16">Mar 2:16</reference>. He vindicates his conduct, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.17">Mar 2:17</reference>. Vindicates his disciples, who are accused of not fasting, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.18-Mar.2.22">Mar 2:18-22</reference>; and for plucking the ears of corn on the Sabbath day, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.23-Mar.2.26">Mar 2:23-26</reference>; and teaches the right use of the Sabbath, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.27">Mar 2:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.2.28">Mar 2:28</reference>. <div eID="gen39142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39143" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39144" type="x-p"/> In the house - The house of Peter, with whom Christ lodged when at Capernaum. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.4.13">Mat 4:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.8.13">Mat 8:13</reference>.
entries.987a87b942349a2ddec531a5689bf068330c2e45: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39145" type="x-p"/> So much as about the door - Meaning the yard or court before the house. <div eID="gen39145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39146" type="x-p"/> Preached The Word - Τον λογον. The doctrine of the kingdom of God; for so ὁ λογος is repeatedly used.
entries.f509aff5141c38160047fa3bcdf3606b5ca9c33d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen39146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39147" type="x-p"/> One sick of the palsy - A paralytic person. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.9.2">Mat 9:2</reference> (note), etc. <div eID="gen39147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39148" type="x-p"/> Borne of four - Four men, one at each corner of the sofa or couch on which he lay: this sick man appears to have been too feeble to come himself, and too weak to be carried in any other way.
entries.7278c4b086ccc44e108b5a58c1586fd28fe17c5f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen39148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39149" type="x-p"/> They uncovered the roof - The houses in the east are generally made flat-roofed, that the inhabitants may have the benefit of taking the air on them; they are also furnished with battlements round about, <reference osisRef="Deu.22.8">Deu 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jdg.16.27">Jdg 16:27</reference>; and <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.2">2Sam 11:2</reference>, to prevent persons from falling off; and have a trap door by which they descend into the house. This door, it appears, was too narrow to let down the sick man and his couch; so they uncovered the roof, removed a part of the tiles; and having broken it up, taken away the laths or timber, to which the tiles had been attached, they then had room to let down the afflicted man. See <reference osisRef="Luk.5.19">Luk 5:19</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Mat.10.27">Mat 10:27</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mat.24.17">Mat 24:17</reference> (note).
entries.4620b9cd1f47a7c3deae9e11cf89d562a9975d58: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen39149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39150" type="x-p"/> Why doth this man thus speak blasphemies? - See this explained <reference osisRef="Mat.9.3">Mat 9:3</reference> (note), etc.
entries.dedfd2374484a2c714444dc1d98f26330085072e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen39150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39151" type="x-p"/> He - took up the bed - The words of Prosper, on this place, are worthy of notice: - "What is sin but a deplorable fall, a grovelling on the earth, a repose in the creature, often followed by a universal palsy of the soul; namely, an utter inability to help itself, to break off its evil habits, to walk in the ways of God, to rise or to take one good step towards him? Grace can repair all in a moment: because it is nothing but the almighty will of God, who commands and does whatever he commands."
entries.82757829a0c5ef482478b913a2cf68ecd29cccc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen39151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39152" type="x-p"/> Levi - The same as Matthew; he appears to have been a Jew, though employed in the odious office of a tax-gatherer. For an account of his call, see his Gospel, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.9">Mat 9:9</reference>, etc.
entries.789634b6057719ca53dbfce7214b4f6ed0e3d59f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen39152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39153" type="x-p"/> Sinners - By ἁμαρτωλοι, the Gentiles or heathens are generally to be understood in the Gospels, for this was a term the Jews never applied to any of themselves, See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.9.10">Mat 9:10</reference>. <div eID="gen39153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39154" type="x-p"/> How is it that he eateth - Some very good MSS., several versions, with Chrysostom and Augustin, read, Why doth Your Master eat?
entries.4a258beba182c0ae42c175af88ad7eafb76b3ba0: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen39154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39155" type="x-p"/> To repentance - This is omitted by ABDKL, twenty-seven others; both the Syriac, Persic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Gothic, Vulgate; six copies of the Itala; Euthymius and Augustin. Griesbach has left it out of the text; Grotius, Mill, and Bengel approve of the omission. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.9.13">Mat 9:13</reference> (note). I leave it as in the parallel place above quoted. Properly speaking, the righteous cannot be called to repentance. They have already forsaken sin, mourned for it, and turned to God. In the other parallel place, <reference osisRef="Luk.5.32">Luk 5:32</reference>, all the MSS. and versions retain μετανοιαν, repentance.
entries.3adddc5f5057db5875c153d1f6bdcc2d4cfeb2f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen39155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39156" type="x-p"/> Why do the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast - See this largely explained on <reference osisRef="Mat.9.14">Mat 9:14</reference> (note), etc. The following vices are very common to Pharisees. <div eID="gen39156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39157" type="x-p"/> 1. They are more busied in censuring the conduct of others than in rectifying their own. <div eID="gen39157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39158" type="x-p"/> 2. They desire that every one should regulate his piety by theirs; and embrace their particular customs and forms of devotion. <div eID="gen39158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39159" type="x-p"/> 3. They speak of and compare themselves with other people, only that they may have an opportunity of distinguishing and exalting themselves. <div eID="gen39159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39160" type="x-p"/> On the nature, times, and duration of fasting, see <reference osisRef="Mat.6.16">Mat 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.9.15">Mat 9:15</reference>.
entries.2d2a5d1b54d933f00145948e03604aaf7f14f989: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen39160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39161" type="x-p"/> Can the children of the bride-chamber fast while the bridegroom is with them? - Among the Hindoos, large parties of friends, belonging both to the bride and bridegroom, attend on both during the wedding day; on the following day, when the bridegroom leaves the house of his father-in-law, the attendants are filled with sorrow, especially the near relations. - Ward's Customs.
entries.b31006860fd2d190fb7116155dc388f5f2dc3dc0: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen39161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39162" type="x-p"/> In those days - But instead of εν εκειναις ταις ἡμεραις, many of the best MSS. and versions read, εν εκεινῃ τῃ ἡμερᾳ, in that day; viz. the day in which Jesus Christ should be delivered up to the Jews and Gentiles. Mill and Bengel approve of this reading, and Griesbach adopts it. The former part of the verse seems to vindicate the common reading.
entries.4232e4595517e0c657e691c7135a3b8e0cd9a46b: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen39162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39163" type="x-p"/> No man - seweth - See <reference osisRef="Mat.9.16">Mat 9:16</reference>. No man seweth a piece of unscoured cloth upon an old garment. In the common editions this verse begins with και, and, but this is omitted by almost every MS. and version of note. The construction of the whole verse is various in the MSS. The translation given here, and in <reference osisRef="Mat.9.16">Mat 9:16</reference>, is intelligible, and speaks for itself.
entries.ca949e00d3b1cc0b05d69768174792f71116b6db: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen39163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39164" type="x-p"/> Went through the corn fields - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.12.1">Mat 12:1</reference> (note).
entries.f9bfca24d68156ebc247bbd7f6a711f525ba9edf: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen39164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39165" type="x-p"/> The days of Abiathar the high priest - It appears from <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1">1Sam 21:1</reference>, which is the place referred to here, that Ahimelech was then high priest at Nob: and from <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.20">1Sam 22:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">1Sam 23:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.16">1Chr 18:16</reference>, it appears that Abiathar was the son of Ahimelech. The Persic reads Abimelech instead of Abiathar. Theophylact supposes that Abiathar was the priest, and Ahimelech or Abimelech the high priest, and thus endeavors to reconcile both the sacred historians. Others reconcile the accounts thus: Ahimelech was called Ahimelech Abiathar, אב ab, father, understood; and Abiathar was called Abiathar Ahimelech, בן ben, son, understood. Probably they both officiated in the high priesthood; and the name of the office was indifferently applied to either. <div eID="gen39165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39166" type="x-p"/> Shew-bread - See <reference osisRef="Mat.12.4">Mat 12:4</reference>.
entries.8b7c1c189bc909ec5b3e36a8342424849dd2dc9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen39166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39167" type="x-p"/> The Sabbath was made for man - That he might have the seventh part of his whole time to devote to the purposes of bodily rest and spiritual exercises. And in these respects it is of infinite use to mankind. Where no Sabbath is observed, there disease, poverty, and profligacy, generally prevail. Had we no Sabbath, we should soon have no religion. This whole verse is wanting in the Codex Bezae, and in five of the Itala.
entries.5ed8c2708af12dc5772741d14a511fc54201e562: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen39167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39168" type="x-p"/> The Son of man is Lord - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.12.7">Mat 12:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.12.8">Mat 12:8</reference> (note). Some have understood this as applying to men in general, and not to Christ. The Son of man, any man is Lord of the Sabbath; i.e. it was made for him, for his ease, comfort, and use, and to these purposes he is to apply it. But this is a very harsh, and at the same time a very lax, mode of interpretation; for it seems to say that a man may make what use he pleases of the Sabbath; and, were this true, the moral obligation of the Sabbath would soon be annihilated. <div eID="gen39168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39169" type="x-p"/> God ordained the Sabbath not only to be a type of that rest which remains for the people of God, but to be also a mean of promoting the welfare of men in general. <div eID="gen39169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39170" type="x-p"/> The ordinances of religion should be regulated according to their end, which is the honor of God, and the salvation of men. It is the property of the true religion to contain nothing in it but what is beneficial to man. Hereby God plainly shows that it is neither out of indigence or interest that he requires men to worship and obey him; but only out of goodness, and to make them happy. God prohibited work on the Sabbath day, lest servants should be oppressed by their masters, that the laboring beasts might have necessary rest, and that men might have a proper opportunity to attend upon his ordinances, and get their souls saved. To the Sabbath, under God, we owe much of what is requisite and necessary as well for the body as the soul.  <chapter eID="Mark.2"/> <div eID="gen39170" type="x-p"/>

entries.811b3d3016a55bbe7cb79c03e133d2a181bc94be:
MARK CHAPTER 2

Verse 1. Into Capernaum. Mt 4:13.

After some days. The number of days is not known. Probably he remained long enough in the desert to heal the sick that were brought to him, and to give instructions to the multitudes that attended his preaching. Capernaum was not the city mentioned in Mk 1:45, and it is probable that there was no difficulty in his remaining there and preaching.

And it was noised, etc. He entered the city, doubtless, privately; but his being there was soon known; and so great had his popularity become, that multitudes pressed to hear him.
entries.6cf05c9b409099e5e740ccada3d4ba197d8750fd:
Verse 2. So much as about the door. In the court or yard before the door. They could not get near enough to hear him.

Preached the word unto them. The word of God; the revelation or doctrine which he came to deliver, called the word; and the word of God, because it was spoken or revealed by God. Compare Acts 6:2-7.
entries.962996cf22fdbba4a58915b8fadb482e2a93aa51:
Verses 3-12. Mt 9:2, also Mt 9:3-8.

Borne of four. Borne on a couch. Mt 9:2 by four men.

(f) "And they come" Mt 9:1, Lk 5:18
entries.468b29febd922e6b896d93eba6119a681477f1ac:
Verse 4. The press. The crowd, the multitude of people. Jesus was probably in the large open area, or hall, in the centre of the house. Mt 9:2. The people pressed into that area, and blocked up the door, so that they could not have access to him.

They uncovered the roof where he was. Mt 9:2. Houses were flat. In cities they joined each other, and the roofs constituted an agreeable place for walking. It is not improbable that they ascended a neighbouring house, and came over the hall, where Jesus was. They removed the curtain or awning, drawn over the area, where Jesus was, so that they might let the man down before him.

When they had broken it up. When they had removed the awning, and a part of the banisters, so that they could let the man down.
entries.e9047e9ea1ad5e6fc8d22ccf9583db39dcf724eb:
Verse 5. Their faith. Their confidence, or belief, that he could heal him.

Son. Literally, child. The Hebrews used the words son and child with a great latitude of signification. They were applied to children, to grandchildren, to adopted children, to any descendants, to disciples, followers, young people, and to dependents. Mt 1:1. In this place, it denotes affection, or kindness. It was a word of consolation:--an endearing appellation, applied by the Saviour to the sick man, to show his compassion, to inspire confidence, and to assure him that he would heal him.

(g) "saw their faith" Acts 14:9, Eph 2:8
entries.d2115d2d92deaa3c7ce7682f97a2ead0002ddd90:
Verse 12. We never saw it on this fashion. Literally, "we never saw it so." We never saw anything like this.

(k) "We never" Jn 7:31, 9:32
entries.ceb97cea08b3001c4a697a5c931e09051733821a: Verse 13. By the sea side. That is, by the sea of Tiberias, on the shore of which Capernaum was situated. Mt 4:13.
entries.fa665cc7e16865276486fbbb143d0e38de8b743f:
Verse 14. Levi the son of Alpheus. The same, undoubtedly, as Matthew the writer of the Gospel. It was not uncommon among the Jews to have two names.

The receipt of custom. Mt 9:9.

(l) "And as" Mt 9:9 (1) "sitting at" or, "at the place where the custom was received"
entries.9e597f3b0bd08b913479cfd9d0281fa29768efd0:
Verse 15. Sat at meat in his house. The words "at meat" are not in the original. The phrase means, as he reclined at his meal "--or "as he was eating." This feast was made by Matthew, in honour of the Saviour. See Lk 5:29.

Publicans. Mt 5:47.

Sinners. Sinners of abandoned character--of the same character that publicans commonly sustained--fit companions of publicans--great sinners.

There were many. That is, many disciples. Their following him, leaving their homes, and going with him from place to place, was proof of their attachment to him, There is no doubt that our Saviour, in the early part of his ministry, was extremely popular. Multitudes of the common people attended him, and gave conclusive evidence that they were his real disciples, And it was only after much opposition and ridicule from the rich, and the great, that he ever became unpopular among the people. Perhaps no preacher has ever attracted so universal attention, and produced so decisive effects on mankind, as our Lord did in his personal ministry.

(m) "And it came to pass" Mt 9:10 (n) "Publicans" Lk 15:1-5
entries.7fd32c3d947a887205e6b17d2fd7988f7169bc49:
Verse 17.

(o) "They that are whole" Mt 9:12,13, Lk 5:31,32 (p) "sinners" Isa 1:18, 55:7, Mt 18:11, Lk 19:10, 1Cor 6:9-11, 1Timm 1:15
entries.21f2837a17ce360e42c16dbcf1f84bc12e0ed60a: Verse 18. And the disciples of John and of the Pharisees used to fast. Were accustomed often to fast. Compare Lk 5:33, 18:12.
entries.39b85f98df14d59284a0a7ca47c2cdc99e05ffce:
Verses 19-22. See Mt 9:15-17

(q) "the bridegroom is with" Mt 25:1
entries.b02a69fa936a1fa683fd371cd1e09d95c43ad87b:
Verses 23-28. See Mt 12:1-8. The corn fields. The fields sown with grain, wheat, or barley. The word corn, in the Bible, refers only to grain of that kind, and never to maize or Indian corn.

To pluck the ears of corn. They were hungry, (Matthew.) They therefore gathered the wheat, or barley, as they walked, and rubbed it in their hands to shell it, and thus to satisfy their appetite. Though our Lord was with them, and though he had all things at his control, yet he suffered them to resort to this method to supply their wants. When Jesus, thus with his disciples, suffered them to be poor, we may learn that poverty is not disgraceful; that God often suffers it for the good of his people; and that he will take care, in some way, that their wants shall be supplied. It was lawful for them thus to supply their wants. Though the property belonged to another, yet the law of Moses allowed the poor to satisfy theft wants when hungry. See De 23:25.

(t) "And it came" Mt 12:1, Lk 6:1 (u) "to pluck" De 23:25
entries.5f82ae012281ed31692e8c5242b2b98b9c7575e7: Verse 24. That which is not lawful. That is, that which they esteemed to be unlawful on the sabbath day. It was made lawful by Moses, without any distinction of days; but they had denied its lawfulness on the sabbath. Christ shows them, from their own law, that it was not unlawful.
entries.2e66f39e1b0e8050ba79e66fb9f418e86b2f4428:

(v) "what David did" 1Sam 21:6
entries.1e312bf9f4dd90621a3528893e3e0011123e942a:
Verse 26. Abiathar the priest. From 1Sam 21:1, it appears that Ahimelech was high priest at the time here referred to. And from 1Sam 23:6, it appears that Abiathar was the son of Ahimelech. Some difficulty has been felt in reconciling these accounts. The probable reason why Mark says it was in the days of Abiathar, is that Abiathar was better known than Ahimelech. The son of the high priest was regarded as his successor, and was often associated with him in the duties of his office. It was not improper, therefore, to designate him as high priest, even during the life of his father, especially as that was the name by which he was afterwards known. Abiathar, moreover, in the calamitous times when David came to the throne, left the interest of Saul, and fled to David, bringing with him the ephod, one of the peculiar garments of the high priest. For a long time, during David's reign, he was high priest, and it became natural, therefore, to associate his name with that of David; to speak of David as king, and Abiathar the high priest of his time. This will account for the fact that he was spoken of, rather than his father. At the same time this was strictly true, that this was done in the days of Abiathar, who was afterwards high priest, and was familiarly spoken of as such; as we say that General Washington was present at the defeat of Braddock, and saved his army; though the title of general did not belong to him till many years afterwards.

Shewbread. Mt 12:4.

(w) "shewbread" Ex 29:32,33, Lev 24:9
entries.66c315c343b815bed36a8c4d5f4f28ac5628c81e:
Verse 27. The sabbath was made for man. For his rest from toil, his rest from the cares and anxieties of the world, to give an opportunity to call off his attention from earthly concerns, and to direct it to the affairs of eternity. It was a kind provision for man that he might refresh his body by relaxing his labours; that he might have undisturbed time to seek the consolations of religion to cheer him in the anxieties and sorrows of a troubled world; and that he might render to God that homage which is most justly due to him as the Creator, Preserver, Benefactor, and Redeemer of the world. And it is easily capable of proof, that no institution has been more signally blessed to man's welfare than the Christian Sabbath. To that we owe, more than to anything else, the peace and older of a civilized community. Where there is no Sabbath, there is ignorance, vice, disorder, and crime. On that holy day, the poor, and the ignorant, as well as the learned, have undisturbed time to learn the requirements of religion, the nature of morals, the law of God, and the way of salvation. On that day, man may offer his praises to the Great Giver of all good, and in the sanctuary seek the blessing of him whose favour is life. Where that day is observed in any manner as it should be, order prevails, morals are promoted, the poor are elevated in their condition, vice flies away, and the community puts on the appearance of neatness, industry, morality, and religion. The Sabbath was, therefore, pre-eminently intended for man's welfare, and the best interests of mankind demand that it should be sacredly regarded as an appointment of merciful heaven, intended for our best good; and, where improved aright, infallibly resulting in our temporal and eternal peace.

Not man for the sabbath. Man was made first, and then the Sabbath was appointed for his welfare, Gen 2:1-3. The Sabbath was not first made or contemplated, and then the man made with reference to that. Since, therefore, the Sabbath was intended for man's real good, the law respecting it must not be interpreted so as to oppose his real welfare. It must be explained in consistency with a proper attention to the duties of mercy to the poor and the sick, and to those in peril. It must be, however, in accordance with man's real good on the whole, and with the law of God. The law of God contemplate man's real good on the whole; and we have no right, under the plea that the Sabbath was made for man, to do anything contrary to what the law of God admits. It would not be for our real good, but for our real and eternal injury, to devote the Sabbath to vice, to labour, or to amusement.

(x) "for man" Neh 9:14, Isa 58:13, Eze 20:12,20 (y) "Therefore" Col 2:16
entries.ac86d7041bafb41bc5798c80abe6e21a9b450ab2:
Verse 28. Therefore the Son of man, etc. Mt 12:8.

(z) "Therefore the Son" Jn 9:14, Eph 1:22, Rev 1:10

entries.9959bb251918717964fd95c83c4b5a5e00e85779: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.2.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.2.24" sID="gen98772" type="section"/> <div sID="gen98773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.2.24">Mark 2:24</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Why do they on the Sabbath what is not lawful?</hi> The Pharisees do not blame the disciples of Christ for <hi type="italic">plucking ears of corn</hi> from a field that was not their own, but for violating <hi type="italic">the Sabbath; </hi>as if there had been a precept to this effect, that famishing men ought rather to die than to satisfy their hunger. Now the only reason for keeping the Sabbath was, that the people, by sanctifying themselves to God, might be employed in true and spiritual worship; and next, that, being free from all worldly occupations, they might be more at liberty to attend the holy assemblies. The lawful observation of it, therefore, must have a reference to this object; for the Law ought to be interpreted according to the design of the Legislator. But this shows clearly the malicious and implacable nature of superstition, and particularly the proud and cruel dispositions of hypocrites, when ambition is joined to hatred of the person. It was not the mere affectation of pretended holiness, as I have said, that made the Pharisees so stern and rigorous; but as they expressly wished to carp at every thing that Christ said or did, they could not do otherwise than put a wrong meaning in cases where there was nothing to blame, as usually happens with prejudiced interpreters. The accusation was brought—according to Matthew and Mark—against our Lord, and—according to Luke—against his disciples. But there is no inconsistency here; for the disciples were in all probability so harassed, that the charge was directed chiefly against the Master himself. It is even possible that the Pharisees first wrangled with the disciples, and afterwards with Christ, and that, in the rage of their malice, they blamed him for remaining silent, and permitting his disciples to break the Sabbath.<div eID="gen98773" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.2.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen98772" osisID="Mark.2.24" type="section"/>

Mark 2:27. The Sabbath was made for man. This Fifth argument is related by Mark alone. The general meaning is, that those persons judge amiss who turn to man’s destruction,
“Lesquels convertissent au dommage et a la ruine de l’homme;”— “who turn to the injury and to the ruin of man.”
the Sabbath which God appointed for his benefit. The Pharisees saw the disciples of Christ employed in a holy work; they saw them worn out with the fatigue of the journey, and partly with want of food; and yet are offended that, when they are hungry, they take a few grains of corn for the support of their wearied bodies. Is not this a foolish attempt to overturn the purpose of God, when they demand to the injury of men that observation of the Sabbath which he intended to be advantageous? But they are mistaken, I think, who suppose that in this passage the Sabbath is entirely abolished; for Christ simply informs us what is the proper use of it. Though he asserted, a little before, that he is Lord of the Sabbath, yet the full time for its abolition
“La vraye saison et le temps opportun de l’abolissement d’iceluy;”— “the true season and appropriate time for the abolition of it.”
was not yet come, because the veil of the temple was not yet rent, (Matthew 27:51.)
